title: Stress-Driven Disproportionation in Oxygen Containing Silicon Nitride Membrane
content: Amorphous silicon nitride (SiNx) films are widely used in closed-cell environmental transmission electron microscopy (ETEM). Typically deposited via low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD), SiNx exhibits low internal stress due to its silicon-rich stoichiometry, making it well-suited for gas or liquid cell experiments. Although commonly referred to as SiNx, these membranes usually contain oxygen impurity which was introduced during oxygen plasma treatment. This mild O2 plasma treatment is a widely adopted step in closed-cell preparation, as it removes carbonaceous residues from chip microfabrication and enhances hydrophilicity, facilitating the drop-casting of aqueous or polar solvent-dispersed materials. Therefore, SiNx can also be labelled as silicon oxynitride (SiOxNy) due to inevitable absorption of O. Furthermore, the amorphous, non-stoichiometric SiNx films will experience oxidation when exposed to O2 at elevated temperatures—a broadly adopted condition in many ETEM experiments. This surface oxidation can lead to compositions ranging from SiO1.25N0.25 to SiO0.5N0.5 for thin (∼10 nm) membranes, while becoming negligible in thicker films (Fig. 1). The oxidation gradient is particularly pronounced in ultrathin (UT) membranes, which are critical for the future of closed-cell ETEM [1].
